teachingReview.heading: Replace enzymes with every fat and protein exposure
teachingReview.body: Pancreatic enzyme replacement provides lipase, protease, and amylase with meals, snacks, formula, and enteral feeds according to product and center plan. Give capsules at the start of eating and distribute during longer meals when directed. Do not crush enteric-coated microspheres or mix them into alkaline food. Persistent symptoms require review of adherence, timing, dose, storage, acid suppression, diet, infection, constipation, and alternate diagnoses. Pancreatic enzyme formulations are not interchangeable. The book distinguishes non-enteric-coated Viokace tablets, which require a proton pump inhibitor, from capsule products such as Creon and Zenpep. Delayed-release capsule particles may be sprinkled onto soft acidic food at pH 4.5 or below, such as applesauce. Swallow the mixture immediately, follow with water, and do not retain the particles in the mouth.

teachingReview.heading: Calculate in lipase units and protect the colon
teachingReview.body: Older children and adults commonly use 500 to 2,500 lipase units per kg per meal and half the meal dose for snacks, or a fat-based method. Doses above 2,500 units per kg per meal or 4,000 units per gram of fat require investigation. Avoid exceeding 10,000 units per kg per day. Very high exposure has been associated with fibrosing colonopathy.
teachingReview.review: All original claims preserved. New handling clauses verified with742and96; full body still includes detailed feeding/modern screening/nutrition/GI/bone/liver/cancer rules not fully established in this source scope.

teachingReview.heading: Individualize nutrition in the modulator era
teachingReview.body: Track growth, weight history, body composition, strength, pulmonary status, intake, malabsorption, food access, and cardiometabolic risk. Many patients need energy-dense intake, salt, and CF-specific fat-soluble vitamin replacement, but highly effective modulators can alter weight and metabolic risk. Do not preserve a universal high-calorie prescription when the patient's current phenotype has changed.

teachingReview.heading: Screen for endocrine and GI complications
teachingReview.body: Annual 75 g oral glucose tolerance testing begins by age 10 for CF-related diabetes screening because A1c alone can miss disease. Insulin remains standard treatment for established CFRD. Monitor constipation and distal intestinal obstruction, reflux, liver disease, gallbladder disease, pancreatitis in pancreatic-sufficient phenotypes, bone health, and CF-specific colorectal cancer risk using current age and transplant guidance.

teachingReview.heading: Detect and treat cystic fibrosis-related diabetes
teachingReview.body: Annual two-hour 75 g oral glucose tolerance testing begins by age 10 because A1c alone can miss postprandial dysglycemia. Illness, systemic glucocorticoids, pregnancy, and enteral feeding require additional glucose assessment. Established CFRD is treated with insulin while preserving nutrition and pulmonary goals.

teachingReview.heading: Protect bone across the lifespan
teachingReview.body: Assess vitamin D, calcium intake, nutrition, weight-bearing activity, glucocorticoid exposure, delayed puberty or hypogonadism, fracture history, transplant status, and bone density according to age and risk. Treatment combines correction of reversible factors with pharmacotherapy when indicated.

teachingReview.heading: Recognize hepatobiliary and kidney risk
teachingReview.body: Follow symptoms, examination, liver chemistry, platelets, imaging, portal-hypertension features, and current CF liver guidance. Review kidney function during nephrotoxic antibiotics, dehydration, aminoglycoside exposure, diabetes, stones, and transplant therapy. Drug doses and monitoring change when organ reserve changes.

teachingReview.heading: Use CF-specific cancer surveillance
teachingReview.body: Adults with CF have increased colorectal cancer risk, especially after solid-organ transplantation. Screening begins earlier and uses CF-specific preparation and intervals under current guidance. New bleeding, anemia, weight loss, obstruction, or persistent bowel change requires diagnostic evaluation rather than waiting for routine screening.
